residualFindings.surface: Selected pale cultivated pilei, stipe grain and dark mature gills are distinct. residualFindings.motion: No mature-body resizing or hyphal expansion remains exposed as development. Separate enlarged location points are a finite teaching overlay, not fitted sporulation, microscopic basidia or a developmental solver.

referenceImage.alt: Snakelocks anemone ( Anemonia viridis ), Arrábida Natural Park , Portugal. The snakelocks anemone is a predator , related to jellyfish (but without a medusa stage in their lifecycle), that ensnares prey of suitable size that comes within reach of its tentacles immobilizing it with the aid of their nematocysts (explosive cells that contain one giant secretory organelle that can deliver a sting). The prey is then transported to the mouth and thrust into the pharynx. This species is widely consumed in Andalusia and is known as ortiguillas de mar (literally, "little sea nettles", because it has urticant properties before it is cooked). The whole animal is marinated in vinegar , coated in a tempura-like batter , and deep-fried in olive oil .

referenceImage.alt: The crab is found in the North Sea, the English Channel, the North-East Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Its shell measures 5 to 6 cm in length and 8 cm in width. It is brownish in colour, with appendages with blue lines and bright red eyes. There are 4 to 5 teeth on the shell on either side of the eyes. Its hind legs, called "swimming legs", have a characteristic flattened shape. Here we see two individuals in the reproductive phase: the male embraces the female during her moulting period, the only period when she is receptive. This embrace can be long. The reproductive period is between February and November. A pink carpet of anemone corinactis, also called jewel anemone, surrounds the crabs. This anemone is present in the English Channel, the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Its color is often bright, with slightly translucent tentacles with a more colorful bulge at their end. Most of the individuals photographed here are closed.

referenceImage.alt: The Atlantic spider crab ( Maja brachydactyla ) is a crustacean. It is found in the waters of the North Sea to the Canaries, on sandy or rocky bottoms, between the surface and 50 m deep. Here, it is a male individual, photographed in the harbor of Brest on a bottom of maërl (accumulation of coralline algae common in Brittany). Its shell, strongly domed and rounded, can measure up to 25 cm long and 18 cm wide. Its legs, with significant hairiness, are long and thin. Note that, unlike other crustaceans, the spider crab has a terminal moult, which has the consequence of stopping its growth abruptly. Its fishing is subject to regulation: see Berne Convention (relating to the conservation of wildlife and natural habitats in Europe): Annex III – Protected species .
